The Mongolian redfin (Chanodichthys mongolicus) is a large-bodied cyprinid native to the Amur River basin and its tributaries, where it occupies the pelagic zone of large rivers and lakes. Field surveys have documented that this predatory species can reach a considerable ultimate total length of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm], a size that distinguishes it from many of its congeners in East Asian freshwater systems. The maximum recorded adult body mass attains approximately 10,960 grams [Wwi = approximately 10,960 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions of large individuals collected during commercial fisheries surveys. This substantial body size is associated with a piscivorous feeding strategy that targets small pelagic fishes and large invertebrates. In contrast, newly hatched larvae are minute, with an estimated wet weight at birth of only 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a mass that corresponds to an egg diameter of roughly 1.3 millimeters and underscores the extreme size disparity across the life cycle.

Sexual maturation in Chanodichthys mongolicus occurs at a body length that marks the transition to reproductive capability. Studies of gonadal development in wild populations indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of 35 cm [Lp = 35 cm], at which point individuals have reached a wet weight at puberty of 437 grams [Wwp = 437 grams], as estimated from length-weight relationships. This size threshold is typical for medium-sized cyprinids and is reached after several growing seasons, reflecting the species' moderate growth rate in temperate river systems. The attainment of sexual maturity is accompanied by the onset of gametogenesis and the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in females and milt-producing testes in males. Field collections of gravid specimens consistently show that individuals below this length lack developed gonads, confirming the 35 cm [Lp = 35 cm] total length as a reliable indicator of reproductive readiness in this population.

Reproductive output in the Mongolian redfin has been characterized using data from captive spawning trials conducted on the closely related congener Chanodichthys dabryi, given the logistical challenges of direct observation of C. mongolicus under controlled conditions. At a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], females can achieve a clutch size of approximately 526 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 526 eggs per spawning event] with a spawning frequency of approximately 365 events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 events per year], yielding a total annual fecundity of approximately 192,000 eggs. This reproductive rate is inferred from the high fecundity typical of pelagic-spawning cyprinids and is supported by oocyte counts from ripe ovaries. The 18 °C [T = 18 °C] thermal regime used in these trials approximates the late-spring and early-summer conditions when natural spawning migrations occur in the Amur River system, linking laboratory findings to field phenology.

Longevity estimates for Chanodichthys mongolicus have been obtained from otolith age readings of wild-caught specimens across its geographic range. The species' documented lifespan reaches 10 years [am = 10 years], a longevity that is relatively typical for medium-to-large-bodied cyprinids inhabiting temperate rivers with distinct seasonal growth marks at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This maximum age of 10 years [am = 10 years] is observed under the thermal conditions of its native habitat, where mean annual water temperatures approximate 18 °C [T = 18 °C] during the active growing season, allowing for consistent annulus formation. The species does not appear to exhibit reproductive senescence, as gravid females near the upper end of the age range are still capable of spawning. In terms of ecological role, the Mongolian redfin functions as a top pelagic predator in the aquatic food webs of the Amur River system. Its large ultimate size, reaching 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] in total length, and corresponding body mass of 10.96 kilograms [Wwi = 10.96 kilograms] allow it to exploit prey items unavailable to smaller sympatric cyprinids. Individuals that achieve puberty at 35 cm [Lp = 35 cm] with a corresponding mass of 437 grams [Wwp = 437 grams] shift from a diet dominated by zooplankton and insect larvae to one consisting primarily of small fish. The hatchling mass of 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams] necessitates an initial period of zooplanktivory before the juvenile fish can begin consuming larger prey. This ontogenetic dietary shift is a key factor structuring competitive interactions within the pelagic fish assemblage and influences recruitment dynamics in the river system.
